cases.question: What can a Java interface contain, and can interfaces be instantiated?
cases.expected_fact: Constants, signatures, default/static methods and nested types; cannot be instantiated.
cases.answer:
Java interfaces can contain only constants, method signatures, default methods, static methods, and nested types. [javaNotesForProfessionals, PDF p. 493]

Interfaces cannot be instantiated. [javaNotesForProfessionals, PDF p. 493]

cases.question: Can a Java class implement multiple interfaces?
cases.expected_fact: A class can implement multiple interfaces.
cases.answer: A Java class can implement multiple interfaces. [javaNotesForProfessionals, PDF p. 493]

cases.question: Which keyword allows an interface to extend another interface?
cases.answer: An interface can extend another interface via the extends keyword. [javaNotesForProfessionals, PDF p. 494]

cases.question: When were interface default methods introduced, and what do they allow?
cases.expected_fact: Introduced in Java 8; allow an implementation inside an interface.
cases.answer:
Interface default methods were introduced in Java 8. [javaNotesForProfessionals, PDF p. 322] [javaNotesForProfessionals, PDF p. 497]

Default methods allow developers to add new methods to an interface without breaking existing implementations. [javaNotesForProfessionals, PDF p. 322] [javaNotesForProfessionals, PDF p. 323]

They provide a default implementation when an implementing class fails to provide one. [javaNotesForProfessionals, PDF p. 322]

They allow specifying an implementation inside an interface to avoid traditional base or abstract classes. [javaNotesForProfessionals, PDF p. 497]

cases.question: What is autoboxing and what is the reverse conversion called?
cases.expected_fact: Automatic primitive-to-wrapper conversion; reverse is unboxing.
cases.answer:
Autoboxing is the automatic conversion that the Java compiler makes between primitive types and their corresponding object wrapper classes. [javaNotesForProfessionals, PDF p. 545]

The reverse conversion going from object wrapper classes to primitive types is called unboxing. [javaNotesForProfessionals, PDF p. 545]

cases.question: Why does unboxing a null Integer cause a NullPointerException?
cases.expected_fact: A primitive int cannot contain null.
cases.answer: Unboxing a null Integer causes a NullPointerException because a primitive type cannot have a null value. [javaNotesForProfessionals, PDF p. 546]

cases.question: When should StringBuffer be used instead of StringBuilder?
cases.expected_fact: When a thread-safe version of StringBuilder is required.
cases.answer: StringBuffer should be used only when a thread-safe version of StringBuilder is required. [javaNotesForProfessionals, PDF p. 94]

cases.question: Does try-with-resources close resources when an exception exits the block?
cases.expected_fact: Resources close when exiting normally or because of an exception.
cases.answer:
Try-with-resources guarantees that resources are closed when the block is exited, whether by usual control flow or because of an exception. [javaNotesForProfessionals, PDF p. 373]

The close call happens no matter how the block completes. [javaNotesForProfessionals, PDF p. 420]
